newsitem.title: CONGO: U.S., Britain scale down Zaire evacuation watch.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Britain scale down Zaire evacuation watch.

text.p: The United States and Britain said on Sunday they were scaling down their forces on standby in Congo to evacuate foreigners from Zaire where rebels were consolidating their hold over the capital Kinshasa.

France and Belgium, which also have troops in Congo's capital Brazzaville across the Zaire river from Kinshasa, said they had no orders to cut their forces. But a Belgian official said his government could decide to pull back troops within the next week.

Both the United States and Britain, accused by the ousted government of president Mobutu Sese Seko of supporting Laurent Kabila's rebels, said they would keep some men in Brazzaville, but if all went well they could be out within a week.

Commander Bob Anderson, spokesman for the U.S. troops deployed for Operation Guardian Retrieval, told Reuters that forward marine units in Brazzaville would return to the USS Kearsarge amphibious assault vessel in the Atlantic off Zaire.
"The situation doesn't warrant keeping these extra guys forward. The situation has gone quiet over there," he said, referring to developments in Kinshasa.
He said the Kearsarge would remain off-shore until further notice in case troops were still needed to protect U.S. nationals and the U.S. embassy.

"One hundred and fifty are to go out of Brazzaville on Monday, I would think we'll all be out of here by Wednesday," he said. "We are still in a position where we can be in Kinshasa in a matter of hours."

Britain expressed similar sentiments. "The situation over there seems to be calming," spokesman Paul Sykes told Reuters. "The infantry soldiers that we have here will be flying back to Gabon starting today."
British soldiers, stripped to the waist, squatted red-skinned in the sun with full backpacks at the airport base as they prepared for the flight.

Sykes said the 230 infantrymen would leave for Gabon's capital Libreville, where they would stay for the time being. A further 160 British service personnel would remain in Brazzaville with four Puma helicopters, speed boats and hovercraft.
France, accused by the rebels of propping up Mobutu, and Belgium, Zaire's former colonial ruler, said they were keeping their forces on alert in Congo until the situation in Kinshasa was more stable.
Belgium has 700 service personnel split between Brazzaville and Congo's port of Pointe Noire. An estimated 1,500 Belgians live in Kinshasa.
"A departure is not on the agenda. It takes a political decision," spokesman Didier Deweerdt told Reuters, adding that a planned May 24 troop rotation was still on.
A spokesman for Belgium's national defence ministry, Ronny Vandenbroele, said the government could decide to call back most troops over the next week.
He told the Belgian news agency Belga that a small contingent would stay behind to guard military materiel until it was shipped back to Belgium.
France has a force of 300 in Congo, of whom 170 are combat troops, mostly from the Foreign Legion.
"As long as there are still any of Mobutu's forces in circulation there is a possible risk for our expatriates," Captain Alexis Jaraud told Reuters.
"Even if we have the impression things are calming down we won't change the numbers until we receive orders from the president of the republic (Jacques Chirac)."
